#PhotonMatrix #LaserMosquitoKiller #Lidar","transcript":"This thing tracks mosquitoes the way an air defense system tracks aircraft, then shoots them down with a laser. It is called Photon Matrix from a startup in Changzhou in eastern China. A lidar sweeps a flat fan of light across the room, constantly measuring how far away the background is. When something small crosses that plane, the distance reading changes. If the size matches a mosquito, the system fires. The company says it reads a target's distance, orientation and body size in about 3 milliseconds and can handle 30 mosquitoes a second. The laser goes down the same optical path the lidar used, aimed at the wings. Range is a 6 meter radius across a 90 degree scan for insects 2 to 20 millimeters, flying slower than 1 meter per second. There is a visible blue laser version for outdoors and an invisible infrared one for bedrooms. For safety, it needs a solid background inside its range. If it cannot find one, the laser shuts off. The Chinese model costs around 638 dollars, but they're not shipping them yet and not even in production.","onScreenText":"IE EXPLAINS tracks mosquitoes

It just works th","transcript":"GPUs, TPUs, MPUs, these are some of the most important chips powering AI right now, but what actually makes them different? To understand that, you need to understand one thing first. Modern AI is basically doing an enormous amount of matrix multiplication, again and again and again. Neural networks take huge grids of numbers, multiply them together, add the results, and repeat that process billions of times. The difference between all these chips is mostly about how specialized they are for doing that math. Let's start with the CPU. The CPU is the general purpose chip inside almost every computer. It has a relatively small number of very powerful cores designed to do almost anything. Run your operating system, open a webpage, execute some code, respond to your mouse click. A CPU can absolutely run AI models. The problem is that neural networks need the same kind of calculation performed across millions of values at the same time, and CPUs simply weren't designed for that level of parallelism. That's where GPUs came in. GPUs were originally built for graphics. To render a game, your computer needs to perform similar calculations across millions of pixels simultaneously. So instead of a few extremely powerful cores, GPUs have thousands of smaller cores working in parallel. And it turns out that architecture is incredibly good for neural networks too. That's why GPUs became the dominant hardware for training and running large AI models. But GPUs are still fairly general purpose. So what if you build a chip specifically for AI?
